hpi_details: 52M with known asymptomatic MVP experiences sudden rupture of posterior leaflet chordae tendineae during exertion causing acute severe mitral regurgitation and flash pulmonary edema requiring emergent mitral valve repair.
ideas: He thinks he tore a blood vessel in his lung or suffered a massive heart attack from straining too hard during his workout.
concerns: He is terrified that he is suffocating to death and will not survive long enough for his wife to reach the emergency room.
expectations: He hopes to receive immediate high-flow oxygen and an urgent injection to flush the fluid out of his lungs.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Ruptured Chordae Tendineae (Acute Severe Mitral Regurgitation) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Ruptured Chordae Tendineae (Acute Severe Mitral Regurgitation) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Acute severe MR from ruptured chordae is a surgical emergency: hemodynamic stabilization (afterload reduction, possible intra-aortic balloon pump) is a bridge to urgent mitral valve repair, not a substitute for it.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Ruptured Chordae Tendineae (Acute Severe Mitral Regurgitation).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute myocardial infarction with papillary muscle rupture without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Sudden pink frothy sputum during exertion — a classic sign of acute flash pulmonary edema.
management_principles: Stabilize with IV diuretics, vasodilators/afterload reduction, and consider intra-aortic balloon pump if hypotensive; obtain urgent echocardiography to confirm flail leaflet and severity
Emergent cardiothoracic surgery referral for mitral valve repair — delay risks refractory cardiogenic pulmonary edema
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.diagnosis: Ruptured Chordae Tendineae (Acute Severe Mitral Regurgitation)

must_ask.say: What were you doing when the breathlessness suddenly got much worse?
What does the sputum you're coughing up look like?
Have you been told you have mitral valve prolapse before?
How severe is your breathlessness right now?
Can you lie flat, or do you need to sit up to breathe?

history.answer: Doctor, I suddenly can't breathe and I keep coughing up this foamy pink liquid. Please help me, I feel like I'm drowning!
It started out of nowhere about two hours ago while I was moving heavy boxes in the garage. It hit me like a ton of bricks within minutes.
I am completely breathless even while sitting still. I can barely speak a few words at a time without gasping.
It has been relentlessly severe since it hit. I have never had anything like this happen to me before.
I cannot lie flat at all. The moment I try to recline, I feel like I am suffocating, so I have to sit straight up.
Any small movement or talking makes it worse. Nothing makes it better, even resting in this chair.
No, I don't hear any whistling or asthma-like wheezing, just a wet bubbling rattle deep in my chest.
Yes, I have a frequent wet cough that brings up frothy, bubbly phlegm that looks light pink.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or sweats at all.
I feel a tight fullness and pressure because I can't get air, but there is no crushing chest pain or sharp stabbing pain when I breathe.
My heart feels like it is pounding and racing very fast, and I feel a little lightheaded because I can't catch my breath. I haven't passed out, though.
It's not thick red blood, just pink, frothy foam coming up when I cough.
No, my legs look totally normal and I haven't noticed any sudden weight gain over the past few weeks.
No, neither calf is swollen or sore, and I haven't had any recent surgery, long flights, or bed rest.
No, I haven't had unusual tiredness, pale skin, or any bleeding like black stools.
No tingling in my hands or around my lips. I am scared because I genuinely cannot breathe, not having a panic attack.

About ten years ago, a doctor told me I had a slight click or floppy heart valve called mitral valve prolapse, but said it was harmless and never needed treatment. I don't have asthma or any other lung problems.
I work in an office behind a desk. I don't work around chemical fumes, dust, asbestos, or pet birds.
I don't take any regular prescriptions, no blood pressure pills, no inhalers, and no painkillers like ibuprofen.
I thought I must have burst an artery in my lung or had a massive heart attack from pushing myself too hard during exercise.
I feel like I'm literally drowning in my own chest, and I'm terrified I won't make it until my wife gets here.
Other than that minor valve click years ago, I have always been completely healthy with no high blood pressure or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been admitted to a hospital.
I take no prescription medications, no over-the-counter pills, and no herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vape products.
I drink socially, maybe a beer or two on the weekend, but nothing heavy.
I work as an accountant and live in a two-story house with my wife and our son.
No one in my immediate family has had early heart attacks, heart failure, or sudden unexplained deaths.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 140/85 mmHg, heart rate 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 88% on room air, temperature 36.7°C.
The patient is sitting bolt upright, visibly struggling to breathe with accessory muscle use, speaking in truncated phrases, and coughing up pink tinged secretions.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are clear without jaundice.
Elevated jugular venous distension to approximately 5 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees with prominent systolic v waves.
Visible intercostal retractions with breathing; hyperdynamic apical impulse without heaves or thrills.
Dullness to percussion at both lung bases with normal resonance over the upper lung fields.
Diffuse coarse crackles and wet bubbling rales heard bilaterally across the lower and middle lung zones.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with a loud grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur loudest at the apex radiating to the axilla, accompanied by a prominent third heart sound.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender without guarding or rebound tenderness; no palpable hepatomegaly.
No pitting edema observed in either lower extremity.
Calves are supple, symmetric, and non-tender bilaterally with no cords or erythema.
Radial and dorsalis pedis pulses are rapid and bounding bilaterally; no peripheral clubbing.
